La razón principal de tanto frío estaba en la construcción. Los muros de piedra eran excelentes para proteger de ataques, pero pésimos para conservar el calor. Las rendijas, las ventanas sin vidrio y las enormes salas vacías hacían imposible mantener una temperatura agradable.

Durante la Alta Edad Media, la mayoría de lasa casas nobles tenía un solo lugar realmente cálido, el Gran Salón. Allí se encendía un gran fuego en el centro, y el humo salía (como podía) por una abertura en el techo. No había chimenea, ni conductos, así que el humo llenaba la sala y el calor se perdía hacia arriba. Solo quienes se sentaban cerca del fuego podían disfrutar de algo de calor, el resto tiritaba en las sombras.
Con el paso del tiempo, entre los siglos XI y XIII, las cosas empezaron a mejorar. Aparecieron las chimeneas y los conductos de humo, que permitieron calentar habitaciones más pequeñas. Fue una especie de revolución doméstica: los señores y las damas ya no tenían que pasar todo el día en el Gran Salón, sino que podían resguardarse en cuartos privados. Aun así, las chimeneas de la época no era muy eficientes. Los muros de piedra absorbían el calor, las ventanas pequeñas (sin cristales) dejaban pasar el aire y el fuego apenas calentaba un rincón del cuarto. Por esa razón, se usaban tapices en las paredes, que además de decorar ayudaban a mantener el calor dentro.
En Europa Central, hacia el siglo XIV, se inventó una solución mucho más práctica: el Kachelofen, un horno de cerámica que acumulaba calor y lo liberaba poco a poco. Era como una estufa de azulejos, muy duradera y eficiente. Bastaba con encender el fuego un rato y el calor se mantenía durante horas. En países como Alemania, Suiza o Austria, estos hornos convirtieron las frías habitaciones de piedra en espacios acogedores. Muchos castillos que esas regiones todavía conservan algunos de estos sistemas.

If people immediately start thinking Termite Mound when listening to this, that is by design. Termites live in the African savannah and create massive towering structures which work in the exact same way described here to keep their nests cool even through the hottest part of the day. That massive earth tower is not the nest itself, it is literally a giant cooling system made of mud.

Modern Earthship houses run on the same principles and are subsequently banned from being constructed (or at least were last I checked), not because they’re dangerous construction, but because they don’t use the materials, rules or even the grid that every other house we build uses. House construction has become a business with hundreds of MILLIONS of dollars invested in it, with links to the manufacturing of house timber, bricks, concrete, metal and even the power grid, all of it worthless if we all followed the Earthship or even Egyptian model.

Now that said, the Egyptian model would not work everywhere, more temperate climates have a different set of challenges to overcome, but the first, the thick walls absorbing and storing heat is a good baseline no matter the climate.

In ancient, as well as modern, Greek the words for work and slavery are the following :
work = δουλειά (pronounced as douliA)
slavery = δουλεία (pronounced as doulEEa) 

Basically it is the same word. This is also the reason why western Europeans thought that ancient Greek societies were slave-based when in reality slavery as we mean it today was far less prevalent than Europeans think. It was indeed Romans who used massively slavery, millions of slaves. Greeks used modest numbers of slaves but the had also serfs (e.g. the Helots of Messenia and the Penestae of Thessalia were technically serfs, not chattel slaves). And of course they had landless workers who were paid in salaries (back then usually given in barter exchange, i.e. as food and wine, clothing and other necessary items). As such the term "doulos" meant both the slave as well as the landless worker working for a salary - thus giving the impression that there were far  more slaves than there were actually in reality. The term remained into the Christian era to mean the house servant (free worker paid in a salary of whatever format) and remained up to our days in the female form, "doula" for housemaids. Since housemaids helped in births, the term "doula" passed on in English to refer to midwives of no medical training (i.e. women who assist pregnant women to give birth).

Note too that indeed the term "scholae" initially did not  mean the school but rather the free time. Since ancient Greeks loved to seek education in their free time, e.g. by going to gymnasiums where they trained physically but also attended the lectures of philosophers, the term "scholae" rose by Hellenistic-Roman Era to mean what we mean today with "school".  And yet in the Greek language the original term of the word was retained in the verb "scholao" which means to end an activity and enter in free time mode! Usually the verb is used by students at the end of their day at school. LOL! oh how the tables have turned!

I live in a pulp mill town. I remember as a child when we would drive through here how we would rolls the windows up and complain about the smell, we couldn't imagine how anyone could live there. We moved here when I was twelve. When I first moved here, and for decades after I recall people when ask about the smell would quickly tell anyone, enthusiastically,  "it smells like money". The pulp mill was closed two years ago, I'm 50 yo, and I didn't notice the smell was gone until a few wees ago when someone from out of town mentioned it. I can tell you right now that almost to a person the people of this county wish it hadn't closed. It made many people millionaires during the 70's,80's, and 90's. Regular people that worked there for 30 years. It was very common for them to retire with a large, nice home and live very comfortably the rest of their lives. Now there's nothing even remotely as secure and well paying to do in the community. 
 The sad part is that the mill was still very profitable, the reasoning in closing it down is lost upon the community. Especially being that for the particular fiber they produced there was only one other competitor in the industry, and the facility that produces it is in far worse shape than this mill.

Visitors for the night crowded on top of the communal kang platform for a warm night's rest in the most bitter cold of northeast Asian winters.

日本の「非電化工房」で断熱材の研究が行われ、稲藁などの古臭い断熱材も有益で、土に家を埋め込む「ホビットハウス」も一定の温度に保てることが研究されているようです。
これは、戦後の日本の家屋が密閉性が高いが断熱性が低く、エアコンだけで全てカバーしようとした結果であり、昔の時代の断熱性を高くする作りはエアコンに過剰に頼る現代の問題を解決するかもしれません。

Cada legionario debía cargar treinta kilos de equipo en distancias de hasta 20 kilómetros diarios. Esta disposición, también introducida por Mario, les ganó a los legionarios el mote de "mulas de Mario". Su dieta habitual, trigo convertido en sémola o pan, aceite de oliva, vino agrio y carne salada, no estaba planificada para ser apetitosa sino para dar energía. Cuando podían, añadían a esta elementos culinarios de la provincia donde se encontraran. Los descansos eran mínimos, la disciplina brutal (ejem, centinela que se durmiera en su guardia era condenado a morir lapidado) y se procuraba que los legionarios nunca estuvieran ociosos, ya que si no estaban combatiendo estaban trabajando construyendo calzadas o montando fuertes. And it theorizes that the Rpmans did not understand mental stress and PTSD, but they did   Oddly, their interest on Roman camps in part tells that the authors do not understand the Romans.  The camp gave reassurance, it was a 'home' in the snese that it was always the same...  1 mile, 10 miles 1000 miles away they had taken a reassuring 'home' with them.  They had 'neighors' that were the same every night and were organized in small groups which shared tents.  A Contiburnum.  8 Soldiers who lived, ate, slept, cooked together.  A virtual family in their tent.  All of that was designed  to reassure and calm the soldiers.  The US Army studied the most emotionally secure group of soldiers to find how they could create  emotional stability.  The answer..  the Romans had it long long before, a squad of 8 men.  So, No, I don't feel that lessons from this piece lay out real history or explain an orginization which laste nearly 700 years and which changed its methods, dress, tactics, units and entire ways of doing things over that time.
